title: Odyssey Mini Essay V2
description: In this 'Mini-Essay' project, you'll write an introduction and body paragraph analyzing whether Odysseus is truly a hero in The Odyssey by Homer. Heroes represent the most valued qualities of a culture, yet concepts of heroism vary greatly across time and societies. By examining Odysseus's actions through Ancient Greek standards and through a modern lens, you'll craft a well-structured argument supported by textual evidence.

sections.title: Prewriting
sections.description: Before you begin writing your essay, you'll organize your ideas through structured prewriting activities. Prewriting helps you brainstorm, clarify your argument, and select strong evidence before drafting. This planning phase ensures your final essay is focused, well-supported, and logically organized. You'll use tables in your document to develop your hook, background information, thesis statement, topic sentences, evidence from the text, commentary, and concluding ideas. Think of prewriting as creating a blueprint; the more effort you invest here, the stronger your final essay will be

objectives.title: Introduction
objectives.description:
Scroll down in your document to find the Prewriting section. You will see tables to help you plan your introduction paragraph. Fill out each table:

  1. Hook: Write one sentence that grabs the reader's attention and introduces the idea of heroism. Make it interesting so readers want to keep reading. Table - T#01Intro#Hook
  2. Background: Write notes about The Odyssey. Include the title, the author (Homer), and a short summary. Mention at least one character or event from the story. Table - T#02Intro#Background
  3. Thesis: Answer this question in one clear sentence: Is Odysseus truly a hero? This sentence will tell readers your main argument. Table - T#03Intro#Thesis


You can use the AI Helper for idea generation and feedback on the quality of your hook statement. You can find the link in the header of your Google Doc. Top right corner.

sections.title: 2-Paragraph Essay
sections.description:
This is where your writing begins! In this section, you'll write your full draft consisting of two strong paragraphs that analyze whether Odysseus is truly a hero. Each paragraph serves a clear purpose and follows specific academic formatting requirements.


Introduction Paragraph: Begin with a hook to grab your reader's attention, mention the epic's title and author, briefly summarize the story, and end with a strong thesis statement that answers whether Odysseus is a hero.


Body Paragraph: Focus on evidence from The Odyssey that supports your position. Use two well-chosen quotes from Homer's epic, provide commentary that explains each quote both within the text and in relation to modern heroism, and make sure everything ties back to your thesis.


Formatting Requirements: Use 12-point Times New Roman font throughout. Left-align all text and use the tab key to indent the first line of each paragraph. Do not add blank lines between paragraphs—your essay should be continuous from introduction through body paragraph. Proper formatting demonstrates your ability to follow MLA conventions and produce professional academic writing.


Aim for 350–500 words total.

objectives.title: Body Paragraph
objectives.description:
Write your body paragraph now. This paragraph proves your thesis using evidence from The Odyssey.

Your paragraph should include these parts in this order:

  1. Indent the first line in this paragraph.
  2. Topic Sentence: Write one sentence that states your main point about Odysseus and connects to your thesis.
  3. Evidence #1: Give a quote from The Odyssey. Before the quote, explain what is happening in the story.
  4. Commentary #1.1 - Inside the Story: Write 1-2 sentences explaining what this quote shows about Odysseus's actions or character in the story.
  5. Commentary #1.2 - Real World: Write 1-2 sentences explaining how this connects to heroes or leadership in today's world.
  6. Evidence #2: Give a second quote from The Odyssey. Again, explain what's happening in the story before you share the quote.
  7. Commentary #2.1 - Inside the Story: Write 1-2 sentences explaining what this second quote shows about Odysseus in Homer's epic.
  8. Commentary #2.2 - Real World: Write 1-2 sentences explaining how this connects to modern ideas about heroism.
  9. Concluding Sentence: End with 1-2 sentences that restate your thesis and explain why your points matter.


Length: 7–10 sentences

Word count: 125–300 words

Finally, check that your essay follows MLA format and reads smoothly without errors.

`Grading Criteria`
 
1) Evaluate whether the student has completed all required prewriting elements for the introduction paragraph. Check that: (1) a hook idea is present in the prewriting table, (2) background information is drafted (including title, author, and summary), and (3) a thesis statement is written that attempts to answer the prompt. Provide specific feedback on which elements are present and which are missing.

2) Evaluate whether the student has completed all required prewriting elements for the body paragraph. Check that: (1) a topic sentence idea is present, (2) two pieces of evidence are identified or drafted, (3) all four commentary sections are addressed (two per piece of evidence), and (4) a concluding sentence idea is present. Provide specific feedback on which elements are present and which are missing.

3) Check that: (1) the quotes or specific references from The Odyssey in the prewriting tables match or closely align with the quotes used in the body paragraph, (2) both pieces of evidence planned in prewriting are present in the final essay (even if slightly revised), and (3) if completely different quotes appear in the essay compared to prewriting, this indicates the prewriting was not used as part of the writing process. Provide specific feedback on whether the evidence in prewriting connects to the evidence in the essay, noting any major discrepancies that suggest the prewriting and essay were completed separately.

4) Check that: (1) the thesis position (hero vs. not a hero) is consistent between prewriting and the introduction paragraph, (2) the core argument remains the same even if wording has been refined, and (3) if the prewriting thesis and essay thesis take opposite positions or address completely different arguments, this indicates academic dishonesty. Commentary sections should contain ideas about how evidence connects to the thesis (not just blank), distinguish between textual commentary (within the book) and real-world commentary, and demonstrate an attempt to explain rather than just summarize. Provide specific feedback on whether the thesis is consistent between prewriting and essay, and whether commentary planning shows understanding of what commentary requires.

objectives.title: Body Paragraph
objectives.description:
Before submitting, review your body paragraph carefully. Start with a clear topic sentence that elaborates on your thesis and provides focus for your argument about Odysseus's heroism. Locate both quotes and confirm each comes directly from The Odyssey wrapped in "double quotation marks"; not paraphrases or summaries. Check that you introduced each quote with context so readers understand where it comes from and why it matters, and verify that both quotes are relevant to heroism and support your thesis. After each quote, include two separate commentaries: the first explaining how the evidence connects to your thesis within The Odyssey, and the second explaining how it connects to real-world heroism or modern applications. Don't just retell what happened; explain why the evidence matters and how it proves your argument.


Review your concluding sentences to ensure you restate your thesis using different words (not copying from your introduction), summarize your main evidence and arguments without word-for-word repetition, and explain why your position on Odysseus's heroism matters by addressing the broader significance of your analysis. Your conclusion should reinforce your argument, wrap up key points, and help readers understand why this analysis is important.

objectives.title: Quality and Format
objectives.description:
Before submitting, check that your essay uses analytical language and flows smoothly. Begin commentary sentences with explanation starters like "This evidence shows that...", "This fact reveals...", "One can see...", or "It is clear that..." to introduce analysis rather than summary; don't just retell what happened in the quotes. Use transition words (for example, similarly, for instance, in addition, furthermore, however, therefore) to connect ideas within and between sections, showing clear relationships between your evidence and commentary so the essay flows without abrupt jumps. Maintain academic writing conventions by avoiding informal language ("you", "your", "things", "stuff", "very", "really") and first-person phrases ("In this essay, I will..." or "I think..."). Keep a formal, objective tone suitable for literary analysis, and capitalize all proper nouns correctly, including Odysseus, Homer, and The Odyssey.


Verify your formatting meets MLA requirements: use 12-point Times New Roman font throughout, double-space the entire document with no extra space between paragraphs, center-align your title, indent the first line of both paragraphs, and left-align all other text. Check that spelling, punctuation, and capitalization are correct, sentence structure is varied with proper subject-verb agreement, and your writing is clear and readable.

`Grading Criteria`

1) Evaluate the student's use of analytical language and transitions to develop their argument. Check that: (1) commentary sentences use explanation starters (such as "This evidence shows that...", "This fact reveals...", "One can see...", "It is clear that...", "This statement means...") that introduce analysis rather than summary, (2) the student analyzes quotes rather than simply retelling what happened, (3) transition words connect ideas within and between sections (for example, similarly, for instance, in addition, furthermore, another, as a result, therefore, however, although), (4) transitions show clear relationships between evidence and commentary, and (5) the essay flows smoothly without abrupt jumps between ideas.

2) Evaluate whether the student follows academic writing conventions appropriate for literary analysis. Check that: (1) the student avoids informal language including "you", "your", "yours", "things", "stuff", "very", and "really", (2) the student does not use first-person phrases such as "In this essay, I will..." or "In this paragraph, I am going to...", (3) the writing maintains a formal, objective tone suitable for analyzing literature, (4) all proper nouns are capitalized correctly (including character names like Odysseus, places, the title The Odyssey, and the author Homer), and (5) the student avoids using "I" statements throughout the essay as required by the prompt. 

3) Evaluate the formatting, grammar, and mechanical quality of the student's two-paragraph mini-essay. Check that: (1) the essay uses 12-point Times New Roman font throughout, (2) the entire document is double-spaced with no extra space between paragraphs, (3) the title is center-aligned at the top, (4) the first line of both paragraphs (introduction and body) are indented, (5) all other text except the title is left-aligned, (6) spelling, punctuation, and capitalization are correct throughout, (7) sentence structure is varied and demonstrates proper subject-verb agreement, and (8) the writing demonstrates clarity and readability appropriate for academic work.
